Body Surface Temperature

By Treatment
Flank body surface temperature (right and left flank averaged; one model with treatment and capture time) was affected by treatment (p = 0.006). EMMs ± SE were 36.29 ± 0.44 °C in S+W+, 36.43 ± 0.44 °C in S+W−, 38.37 ± 0.44 °C in S−W+ and 38.67 ± 0.44 °C in S−W− (lowest to highest: S+W+, S+W−, S−W+ and S−W−; Table 3). Each shaded treatment was cooler than each unshaded treatment (S+W+ vs S−W+: p = 0.019; S+W− vs S−W−: p = 0.014; S+W+ vs S−W−: p = 0.011; S+W− vs S−W+: p = 0.025), while water access made no difference within shade (S+W+ vs S+W−: p = 0.985) or without shade (S−W+ vs S−W−: p = 0.876). The factorial model confirms this: shade p = 0.001, water p = 0.484, shade × water p = 0.788.

Effect of Coat Color
Adjusted for treatment, capture time and period, coat color affected flank temperature in the mixed model (F(2, 142.2) = 6.11, p = 0.003). EMMs ± SE were 37.92 ± 0.36 °C for black, 37.42 ± 0.34 °C for red and 36.69 ± 0.41 °C for cream coats (black vs cream: p = 0.002; black vs red: p = 0.150; red vs cream: p = 0.055). title: Methods
text:
2 · Experimental Design
The experiment followed a 4 × 4 Latin square design over four 5-day periods (two adaptation days, one rest day, two data collection days), repeated at 30-day intervals. Eight animals (four Braford, four Jersey) were assigned to each of four groups, rotating across treatments each period.

Code
Description




Shade + ad libitum water
S+W+

Shade + restricted water
S+W−
Shade and pasture ad libitum; water available 1h/day (12:00–12:30 and 17:30–18:00)

No shade + restricted water

Paddocks were managed under the Voisin Rational Grazing system and subdivided with temporary fencing (1,300 m² per subdivision; 162 m²/animal). Animals were moved daily at 06:50h. Shaded subdivisions provided 390 m² of tree canopy per subdivision (48.7 m²/animal). Six paddocks were shaded by Inga edulis trees planted in rows (3 m between plants; 20 m between rows).
For restricted water treatments, animals were led through a 5 m-wide corridor to troughs located 100 m from the paddocks at the designated times, reflecting practices common on farms without in-paddock water.

title: Methods
text:
3 · Behavioral Observations
Behavioral assessments ran continuously from 07:00 on one day to 07:00 the following day (48h per period). Scan sampling was performed instantaneously every 10 minutes across all four groups simultaneously, yielding 24 scans per hour. Scan 1 = 07:00h; Scan 12 = 18:00h (daytime); Scan 13 = 19:00h; Scan 24 = 06:00h (nighttime). Observers were trained and passed two reliability tests reaching ≥95% agreement before data collection.
Behaviors recorded followed the ethogram of the Laboratory of Applied Ethology (LETA/UFSC):







Behavior
Definition




Grazing
Head lowered to pasture height, apprehending forage, stationary or moving


Ruminating
Lateral mandibular chewing, lying or standing, head at or above body level


Idle standing
Standing or lying without body movement


Lying idle
Lying without body movement


Lying ruminating
Ruminating while lying


Drinking
Lips submerged in water with swallowing movements


Other
Any behavior not described above



For analysis, behaviors were grouped as:

Grazing = grazing only
Other = other behaviors (analysed separately; no longer added to grazing)
Lying = lying idle + lying ruminating
Standing = idle standing + standing ruminating
Ruminating = ruminating in any posture (standing + lying)

title: Methods
text:
4 · Drinking Behavior and Water Intake
Drinking events were recorded at each trough visit: animal identity, start and end time, number of sips, and drinking duration (s). Sip rate (sips/s) was derived as sips ÷ duration. Surveillance cameras (Intelbras®) were installed at each trough and recorded continuously during observation days to capture nighttime visits without observer presence. Time spent with head raised mid-bout was discounted from drinking duration.
Daily water intake was measured using water meters (Unimag®, precision 0.01 L) installed at the inlet of each trough, recorded at 07:00 and 19:00h. Consumption volumes were corrected for daily precipitation and evaporation relative to trough surface area. All troughs were supplied from the same source, controlled by a float valve. Daily group intake was divided by 8 to estimate per-animal consumption.

title: Methods
text:
5 · Thermal Comfort
Climatic variables (air temperature, relative humidity, wind speed, precipitation) were collected at the FER–UFSC Meteorological Station (ID 1036), 300 m from the experimental area.
Black globe temperature was recorded every 5 minutes from 08:00 to 18:00h using Data Loggers (Elitech® RC-4HC) installed at 1 m height in shaded and unshaded paddocks.
Wet-Bulb Globe Temperature (WBGT) was calculated hourly as a composite thermal stress index for cattle. Thresholds follow Baeta & Souza (2010): ≤ 74 comfort; > 74–78 alert; > 78–84 danger; > 84 critical.
Thermal Radiation Load (TLR) was derived from the Stefan-Boltzmann equation applied to mean radiant temperature (W/m²).
Soil surface temperature was measured hourly from 09:00 to 18:00h using an infrared thermometer (Simpla® TI-55; range −55 to 550°C; precision ±1°C) at three location types: full sun, sun between trees, and under tree canopy (shade). Measurements in shaded paddocks were taken at four shaded and four unshaded points; in unshaded paddocks at four random points. All readings were taken by the same person following a standardized protocol.

title: Methods
text:
6 · Thermography
Non-invasive body surface temperature was assessed for 16 cows (four per group: two Braford, two Jersey). Thermographic images were captured at 3 m distance at 10:00, 13:00, and 16:00h on collection days using an infrared camera (Flir® T640; emissivity = 0.98). Four anatomical regions were assessed: right flank, left flank, eye, and udder.
Images were analyzed in Flir Thermal Studio® to extract minimum, mean, and maximum temperatures per region. Body surface temperature was calculated as (mean + maximum) / 2 following Montanholi et al. (2008); minimum values were excluded due to greater environmental influence. For flank analyses, right and left flank values were averaged per animal, day and capture time.

title: Methods
text:
7 · Statistical Analysis
All analyses were performed in R (R Core Team, 2023) using lme4, lmerTest, and emmeans. Code is available via the Code buttons on each results page.

Experimental unit and random structure
The design is a 4 × 4 Latin square (4 groups of 8 cows × 4 periods, 2 collection days per period). The experimental unit is group × period (16 units), not the animal-hour, so every animal-level model includes a group × period random effect in addition to group, animal and day/hour. Period is a fixed effect and group is random:
\[
Y = \text{treatment} + \text{period} + (1 \mid \text{group}) + (1 \mid \text{group:period}) + (1 \mid \text{animal\_id}) + (1 \mid \text{day} / \text{hour}) + \varepsilon
\]
Models that did not converge or were singular were refitted with the bobyqa optimizer; random terms whose variance was estimated as zero were then dropped (never group × period). Each results page lists the models affected.


Linear mixed models (LMM)
Continuous outcomes were analyzed with lmer() (lmerTest), with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom for all tests and EMMs. Behavioral outcomes (scans/h of grazing, other, lying, standing and ruminating) were modelled separately for daytime and nighttime. Drinking duration was modelled on the log scale and is reported as back-transformed geometric means. Water intake is a group-day measure (group intake ÷ 8) and was modelled with group and group × period as random effects (day within group × period is the residual). Thermography models used flank temperature averaged over the right and left flank, with treatment and capture time in the same model, and (1 | group) + (1 | group:period) + (1 | animal_id) + (1 | day).


Generalized linear mixed models (GLMM)
Daily drinking events per animal were counted on the complete animal × day grid (animal-days without drinking entered as 0) and modelled with a Poisson GLMM (glmer()). The Pearson dispersion ratio was checked; when it was clearly below 1, a generalized Poisson GLMM (glmmTMB, genpois) was fitted as a sensitivity check. Sips per drinking event were modelled with a Poisson GLMM, switching to a negative binomial GLMM (glmmTMB, nbinom2) when overdispersed. Back-transformed rates and rate ratios are reported.


Factorial models
The four treatments form a 2 × 2 factorial. Each outcome (except shade use) was also modelled as shade * water + period with the same random structure, and shade, water and shade × water were tested with emmeans::joint_tests(). Where the interaction had p < 0.10, simple effects (shade within water, water within shade) are reported.


Experimental-unit sensitivity analysis
As a check on the mixed models, every behavior, drinking and intake outcome was averaged to one value per group × period (16 values) and analysed as a classic Latin square with lm(): y ~ treatment + period + group and y ~ shade * water + period + group (6 error df). Coat color and breed, which vary only between animals, were tested in mixed models that keep the animal random effect and also on one mean per animal (n = 16).


Estimated marginal means and comparisons
Estimated marginal means (EMMs) and pairwise contrasts were obtained using the emmeans package with Tukey adjustment for multiple comparisons. Model-based results are reported as EMM ± SE; descriptive tables report raw mean ± SD. Significance is indicated as: *** p < 0.001; ** p < 0.01; * p < 0.05; . p < 0.1; ns p ≥ 0.1. Residual diagnostics (residuals vs fitted and QQ plots for LMMs; DHARMa simulated residuals for GLMMs) are shown in collapsible sections on each results page.


Shade use
Proportion of daytime scans recorded in shade was modeled as a continuous outcome using LMM, restricted to S+ treatments (S+W+ and S+W−). The 12:00h and 17:00h scan blocks, when W− animals were taken to the trough corridor (12:00h and 17:30–18:00h), were excluded for both S+ treatments.
Code

The problem
Cattle in tropical and subtropical pasture systems routinely face periods of intense thermal stress. During the hottest hours of the day, animals face a behavioral trade-off: continue grazing and risk overheating, or seek shade and reduce dry matter intake.
When shade is not available — or when water access is restricted — this trade-off becomes a welfare problem. Animals may reduce voluntary grazing, increase time standing idle, or alter drinking patterns in ways that affect both productivity and wellbeing.
What is less understood is how the combination of shade and water availability shapes cattle behavior and thermal comfort across a full 24-hour cycle. Nocturnal compensatory grazing, drinking dynamics, and body surface temperature responses to restricted resources are rarely studied together.
This experiment set out to answer that directly.

The experiment
Thirty-two cows — 16 Braford and 16 Jersey — were assigned to four treatment combinations across a 4 × 4 Latin square design, managed under Voisin Rational Grazing in silvopastoral paddocks at the Ressacada Experimental Farm, UFSC.

The experiment was conducted at the Ressacada Experimental Farm (FER–UFSC), Florianópolis, Brazil (27°40’25” S; 48°32’30” W), from December 2021 to April 2022.
This research was conducted under the Voisin Rational Grazing system, which structures pasture use around animal welfare and soil recovery.
Shade trees (Inga edulis) were established in rows across experimental paddocks, creating a silvopastoral layout that mirrors real-world agroecological farm conditions in southern Brazil.
Animal procedures were approved by the Ethics Committee on Animal Use (CEUA) of UFSC under Protocol 857122042.

Data collection

Black globe thermometers, soil surface measurements, and meteorological station data characterized the thermal environment continuously.
Thermographic images captured body surface temperatures at three time points daily.
Behavioral scans were recorded every 10 minutes across full 24-hour cycles.
Drinking events were recorded continuously.

Note



This page synthesizes results from the Thermal Comfort and Behavior pages. Every value is computed from the models on those pages when the site is rendered. Model results are estimated marginal means (EMMs) from mixed models with group × period (16 units) as the experimental unit; behavioral percentages are raw means across animals (Table 2 of the Behavior page).

title: Key Findings
section: 1 · Shade Reduced Thermal Load — But Did Not Eliminate Heat Stress
text:
1 · Shade Reduced Thermal Load — But Did Not Eliminate Heat Stress
Shade access reduced black globe temperature by 4.22 °C on average (32.66 °C in sun vs 28.44 °C in shade; p < 0.001), with peak unshaded temperatures reaching 50.7 °C. Radiant thermal load was 21.1% lower under shade (520.4 vs 659.2 W/m²; p < 0.001).
Despite this reduction, thermal stress was not fully eliminated in either condition. Using BGHI thresholds (Baeta & Souza, 2010; comfort ≤ 74, alert > 74–78, danger > 78–84, critical > 84):

Shade reduced critical-threshold hours by 71%, but shaded paddocks still reached danger or critical levels in 47 of 88 recorded hours. Shade alone did not remove heat stress under the conditions observed.
Soil surface temperature followed the same gradient — shade 25.32 °C, sun between trees 30.23 °C, full sun 32.06 °C (shade vs sun between trees: p < 0.001; shade vs full sun: p < 0.001) — so the benefit of shade extended to the ground where cattle lie.

title: Key Findings
section: 2 · Daytime Behavior: Water Restriction Reduced Grazing; Shade Helped Only With Water
text:
2 · Daytime Behavior: Water Restriction Reduced Grazing; Shade Helped Only With Water
Treatment affected daytime grazing (p = 0.002), other behaviors (p < 0.001) and standing (p = 0.001), but not lying (p = 0.481) and ruminating (p = 0.155). In the shade × water factorial models, water access had the clearest effect on daytime grazing (p < 0.001). Shade and water interacted (p = 0.033): shade increased grazing when water was ad libitum (S+W+ vs S−W+: p = 0.014) and had no effect under water restriction (S+W− vs S−W−: p = 0.658).
S+W+ animals grazed the most (76.8% of daytime scans) and stood the least (7.4%). Daytime standing rose with both lack of shade (factorial shade p = 0.005) and water restriction (water p < 0.001), reaching 18.5% of scans in S−W−.






S+W− as the pivotal treatment. Animals with shade but restricted water (S+W−) grazed 66.9% of daytime scans, against 76.8% in S+W+ and 67.6% in S−W−. Under water restriction, shade did not change daytime grazing, so the thermal comfort provided by shade did not offset the effect of restricted water.

title: Key Findings
section: 3 · Nocturnal Grazing Was Highest in S+W−
text:
3 · Nocturnal Grazing Was Highest in S+W−
At night, treatment affected grazing (p < 0.001) and lying (p = 0.010), but not other behaviors (p = 0.077), ruminating (p = 0.989) and standing (p = 0.174). The highest nocturnal grazing was in S+W− (15.6% of night scans). In the factorial model the shade × water interaction was p = 0.094, and shade increased nocturnal grazing under water restriction (S+W− vs S−W−: p < 0.001). This is consistent with S+W− animals recovering at night some of the grazing they lost during the day. Water access on its own did not predict nocturnal grazing (p = 0.274).

title: Key Findings
section: 4 · Water Restriction Changed Drinking Frequency More Than Intake
text:
4 · Water Restriction Changed Drinking Frequency More Than Intake
Counting every animal-day, W+ animals drank 1.8× as often as W− animals (3.14 vs 1.75 events/animal/day; p < 0.001). Daily intake was 22.6 L/animal in W+ and 19.1 L in W− (p = 0.173 in the mixed model; p = 0.047 on group × period means), so the 3.5 L/day gap was not significant in the mixed model.

title: Key Findings
text:
5 · Water-Restricted Animals Used Shade More
Among S+ treatments, animals with restricted water (S+W−) spent a significantly greater proportion of daytime scans in shade than ad libitum animals (59.6% vs 54.7%; p < 0.001). The difference came mainly from the morning (07:00–11:00h: 10.5 percentage points more shade in S+W−), when W− animals could not drink. The 12:00h and 17:00h scan blocks were excluded from this comparison because S+W− animals were in the trough corridor at those times.

title: Key Findings
section: 6 · Body Surface Temperature: Shade Mattered, Water Did Not
text:
6 · Body Surface Temperature: Shade Mattered, Water Did Not
Flank surface temperature (right and left flank averaged) was 36.29 ± 0.44 °C in S+W+ and 36.43 ± 0.44 °C in S+W−, against 38.37 ± 0.44 °C in S−W+ and 38.67 ± 0.44 °C in S−W− (EMM ± SE; treatment p = 0.006). In the factorial model, the shade effect had p = 0.001 and the water effect p = 0.484 (interaction p = 0.788).
Time of day had a large effect: flank temperature was 39.16 ± 0.40 °C at 10:00h, 37.83 ± 0.40 °C at 13:00h and 35.32 ± 0.40 °C at 16:00h (p < 0.001).
Coat color affected surface temperature when tested on one mean per animal (n = 16; F(2, 13) = 6.21, p = 0.013): black 37.92 ± 0.36 °C, red 37.42 ± 0.34 °C and cream 36.69 ± 0.41 °C (EMM ± SE from the mixed model; black vs cream p = 0.010, black vs red p = 0.204). Breed had no detectable effect (F(1, 14) = 0.01, p = 0.919). All red animals were Braford and all black and cream animals were Jersey, so coat and breed effects cannot be fully separated.

title: Key Findings
text:
7 · Integrated Interpretation
Shade lowered the thermal load and the animals’ body surface temperature, and it supported daytime grazing — but only when water was freely available. Water restriction reduced daytime grazing, raised daytime standing, cut drinking frequency, and increased the use of shade in the morning. S+W− animals grazed most at night, which suggests they recovered part of the daytime grazing they lost.
Together, these results indicate that shade and water act through different but interacting pathways: shade changes the thermal microenvironment, while water availability limits how much of that benefit the animals can turn into grazing. Neither resource alone was enough to fully support behavior under the conditions observed.

1 Introduction

[Introduction to be written — see notes below for structure]
The hypothesis of the study was that the availability of water and shade alters the ingestive behavior of cattle, resulting in greater rest time during the hottest periods of the day compared to restricted or no access to these resources. However, during the night, cattle raised with free access to water and shade show greater grazing time, compensating for the reduction of this behavior during the day.
The objectives of the study were:

To evaluate the effect of ad libitum water availability on the diurnal and nocturnal behavior of cows;
To evaluate the effect of shade provision on the diurnal and nocturnal behavior of cows;
To evaluate the effect of ad libitum water availability, combined or not with shade, on the thermal comfort of cows.

text:
2 Methods
Animal procedures were approved by the Ethics Committee on Animal Use (CEUA) of the Federal University of Santa Catarina (UFSC) (CEUA Protocol 857122042).

2.1 Study Site and Animals
The study was conducted at the Bovine Vivarium of the Ressacada Experimental Farm (FER) — Federal University of Santa Catarina, located in Florianópolis, Brazil (27°40’25” S; 48°32’30” W), from December 2021 to April 2022. The experimental area covered 3.2 ha and was divided into twelve paddocks of 2,600 m² each. Six paddocks were shaded by Inga edulis trees planted in rows with 3 m spacing between plants and 20 m between rows. The remaining six paddocks contained pasture only. Forage species present across all paddocks included plants from the genera Brachiaria, Melilotus, Setaria, Axonopus, Cynodon, Panicum, Hemarthria, Desmodium, Trifolium, Lotus, Pennisetum, Arachis, Stylosanthes, Lolium and Paspalum.


2.2 Experimental Design
Thirty-two females of the Braford (mean body weight: 478 ± 44 kg) and Jersey (mean body weight: 385 ± 33 kg) breeds were divided into four groups of eight animals each (four Braford and four Jersey per group). Animals were individually identified with ear tags and numbered on both flanks using non-toxic paint. The experiment was conducted in a 4 × 4 Latin square design over four periods (repetitions), with groups randomly allocated to treatments in each period. Treatments were:



Table 1: Experimental treatments










Code
Treatment
Description




S+W+
Shade + ad libitum water
Paddocks with shade, pasture, mineral supplement and water available 24h


S+W-
Shade + restricted water
Paddocks with shade, pasture and mineral supplement ad libitum; water available only 1h/day (12:00–12:30 and 17:30–18:00)


S-W+

Paddocks without shade, with pasture, mineral supplement and water available 24h


S-W-
No shade + restricted water
Paddocks without shade, with pasture and mineral supplement ad libitum; water available only 1h/day (12:00–12:30 and 17:30–18:00)






Animals were weighed individually at the start and end of each period. Each repetition occurred at 30-day intervals and lasted five days: two days of adaptation, two days of data collection, separated by one rest day. Groups were managed under the Voisin Rational Grazing system [@MachadoFilho2021]. Paddocks (2,600 m²) were subdivided with temporary fencing (1,300 m²), yielding 162 m² of pasture per animal. Animals remained 24h in each subdivision and were moved daily at 06:50h. In shaded treatments, each subdivision included 390 m² of shade area, guaranteeing 48.7 m²/animal.


2.3 Data Collection
Behavioral assessments occurred from 07:00 on one day to 07:00 the following day, on alternate days, totaling 48h of observation per period. Observers underwent training and two reliability tests. During data collection, observers alternated between treatments and animal groups to reduce observational bias. Both reliability tests achieved 95% agreement between observers [@Lehner1996].
Observers were positioned at a distance that allowed observation without interfering with animal behavior. Short-duration behaviors were recorded as events; longer-duration behaviors were classified as states and sampled at regular intervals as instantaneous records [@Altmann1974].

2.3.1 Behavioral Observations
Individual behavioral observations were recorded on field sheets simultaneously across all four groups, noting the animal, paddock location and time. Records were taken instantaneously every 10 minutes, according to Table 2. The ethogram follows definitions adopted by the Laboratory of Applied Ethology (LETA) [@Coimbra2012; @Bica2020; @Sousa2021].

Description




Grazing
Animal with head lowered to pasture height, apprehending forage, stationary or moving


Ruminating
Animal with head at or above body level performing lateral mandibular chewing movements, lying or standing


Drinking
Animal with lips submerged in water performing esophageal and swallowing movements


Walking
Animal in movement with head above pasture level


Standing idle
Animal standing or lying without performing body movements


Mineralizing
Animal licking and ingesting mineral supplement


Other
Any behavior not described above








2.3.2 Water Consumption
Water meters (Unimag®, precision 0.01 L) were installed at the inlet of each trough — between the ball valve and flange — to record consumption per group individually. Troughs were circular plastic reservoirs (Multilit®, 500 L; 0.6 m height × 1.2 m diameter), marked at the upper rim to indicate maximum water level. Consumption was recorded on all observation days at 07:00 and 19:00h. Volume differences were corrected for daily precipitation and total evaporation relative to trough surface area. All troughs were supplied from the same water source, controlled by a float valve.
In the S+W− and S−W− treatments, animals were led through a corridor (5 m wide) to troughs located 100 m from the paddocks at the designated times (12:00–12:30 and 17:30–18:00). These drinking times reflect practices commonly observed on farms that do not provide in-paddock water. In S+W+ and S−W+ treatments, troughs remained available throughout the day.
To reduce human interference with animal behavior and facilitate nighttime observation of drinking events, surveillance cameras (Intelbras®) were installed at each trough, connected to a video storage device, recording continuously during observation days.
Drinking behavior was evaluated as events [@Coimbra2012]: at each trough visit, time, number of sips (G), animal identity (AE), drinking time (TB) and sip rate (TG, sips/second) were recorded. Water intake was considered when the animal had its lips submerged and was performing swallowing movements. Time spent with head raised was discounted and restarted when the animal resumed drinking during the same visit.


2.3.3 Thermal Comfort
Climatic variables — air temperature (TA), relative humidity (RH), wind speed, evaporation, rainfall and sunshine hours — were collected daily at the FER–UFSC Meteorological Station (station ID 1036), located 300 m from the experimental area.
The Black Globe Temperature and Humidity Index (ITGU) was calculated hourly from 09:00 to 18:00h as an indicator of heat stress in cattle. Black globe thermometers were installed in shaded and unshaded paddocks, fixed at 1 m height above ground (approximately the trunk height of a medium-sized cow). Globe temperature (TGN) data were recorded every 5 minutes from 09:00 to 18:00h using a Data Logger (Elitech® RC-4HC).
ITGU was calculated using Equation 1 described by @Buffington1981:
\[
\text{ITGU} = T_{gn} + 0.36 \cdot T_{po} - 41.5
\tag{1}\]
Where: ITGU = Black Globe Temperature and Humidity Index; \(T_{gn}\) = black globe temperature (°C); \(T_{po}\) = dew point temperature (°C).
Dew point temperature (TPO) was calculated using Equation 2 simplified by @Wilhelm1976:
\[
T_{po} = T_a - \frac{(100 - \text{RH})}{5}
\tag{2}\]
Where: \(T_a\) = air temperature (°C); RH = relative humidity (%).
ITGU thresholds follow @Baeta2010: ≤74 = comfort; 75–78 = alert; 79–84 = danger; >84 = critical.
The Radiant Thermal Load (CTR) was calculated using Equation 3 proposed by @Esmay1982:
\[
\text{CTR} = \sigma \times T_m^4
\tag{3}\]
Where: \(\sigma\) = Stefan-Boltzmann constant (5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W/m² K⁴); \(T_m\) = mean radiant temperature (W/m²).
Soil surface temperature (TS) was measured hourly from 09:00 to 18:00h in all treatments using an infrared thermometer (Simpla® TI-55; range −55 to 550 °C; precision ±1 °C; resolution 0.1 °C). In RAL and RAV, measurements were taken at four random points; in SAV and SAL, at eight points (four under tree canopy, four in unshaded areas). All measurements were performed by the same person following a standardized positioning and distance protocol.
For non-invasive assessment of treatment effects on animal body surface temperature, thermographic images were obtained from 16 cows (four per group: two Braford and two Jersey). The anatomical regions assessed were: eye (O), right flank (FD), left flank (FE) and posterior udder (U) [@Montanholi2008; @Sorensen2014]. Animals were photographed at 3 m distance at 10:00, 13:00 and 16:00h during collection days in each period (with the exception of the last day of period 4 due to rain). Images were captured using an infrared thermographic camera (Flir® T640; emissivity coefficient 0.98 for biological tissues, per manufacturer recommendation) and analyzed in Flir Thermal Studio® software to extract minimum, mean and maximum temperatures for each anatomical region. Mean and maximum temperatures were used for analysis; minimum values were excluded due to greater environmental influence [@Montanholi2008; @Salles2016].



2.4 Statistical Analysis
All analyses were performed in R (R Core Team, 2023) using the packages lme4, lmerTest, and emmeans. Descriptive statistics (mean, standard deviation, minimum, and maximum) were computed per treatment group.

2.4.1 Behavioral and Thermal Outcomes
Continuous outcomes (behavioral scan counts, black globe temperature, WBGT, thermal radiation load, soil surface temperature, and body surface temperature) were analyzed using linear mixed models (LMM) fitted with lmer() (lmerTest package, Satterthwaite degrees of freedom):
\[
Y_{ijk} = \alpha_j + (1 \mid \text{animal}_i) +
          (1 \mid \text{day}_k / \text{hour}_{jk}) + \varepsilon_{ijk}
\]
where \(\alpha_j\) is the fixed effect of treatment, shade group (S+/S−), or water group (W+/W−). Random effects included animal identity and observation hour nested within experimental day. Thermography models included animal identity and day/hour nested within day as random effects; water intake models used experimental group and day.


2.4.2 Drinking Event Counts
Daily drinking events per animal were modeled with a Poisson generalized linear mixed model (GLMM) using glmer():
\[
\log(\lambda_{ij}) = \alpha_j + (1 \mid \text{animal}_i) + (1 \mid \text{day}_k)
\]
Back-transformed event rates and rate ratios (W+ vs W−) are reported.


2.4.3 Post-hoc Comparisons
Estimated marginal means (EMMs) and pairwise contrasts were obtained using the emmeans package with Tukey adjustment for multiple comparisons. Significance levels: *** p < 0.001; ** p < 0.01; * p < 0.05; . p < 0.1; ns p ≥ 0.1.

Behavioral Activity Patterns

Daytime Behavior
With group × period as the experimental unit, treatment affected daytime grazing (p = 0.002), other behaviors (p < 0.001) and standing (p = 0.001), but not lying (p = 0.481) and ruminating (p = 0.155) (Table 2; F tests with Satterthwaite df). Pure grazing was highest in S+W+ (76.8% of scans) and lowest in S+W− (66.9%). Standing was lowest in S+W+ (7.4%) and highest in S−W− (18.5%). Other behaviors were a small part of the budget (1.1–2.4% of daytime scans). Within each column of Table 2, values sharing a letter do not differ significantly (Tukey-adjusted, p > 0.05).

In the single-factor models, shaded animals (S+) grazed more during the day than unshaded animals (S−; p = 0.449), lay down more (p = 0.133) and stood less (p = 0.080). Water-restricted animals (W−) grazed less than W+ animals (p = 0.002) and stood more (p = 0.005).
The factorial models (Table 46) separate these effects. For daytime grazing, water had a strong main effect (p < 0.001), shade a weaker one (p = 0.080), and the two interacted (p = 0.033): shade increased grazing when water was available (S+W+ vs S−W+: p = 0.014) but not under water restriction (S+W− vs S−W−: p = 0.658), so water restriction removed the grazing benefit of shade. Daytime standing was affected by both shade (p = 0.005) and water (p < 0.001) without interaction (p = 0.112).


Nocturnal Grazing
At night, treatment affected grazing (p < 0.001) and lying (p = 0.010), but not other behaviors (p = 0.077), ruminating (p = 0.989) and standing (p = 0.174). Nocturnal grazing was higher in shaded than unshaded animals (p = 0.012), whereas water access alone did not predict it (p = 0.274). Among individual treatments, S+W− showed the highest nocturnal grazing (15.6% of scans). In the factorial model the shade × water interaction for nocturnal grazing was p = 0.094: shade increased nocturnal grazing under water restriction (S+W− vs S−W−: p < 0.001) but not with free water (p = 0.196), consistent with compensatory night grazing in S+W−. Nocturnal lying was highest in S−W− (76.5%; shade effect in the factorial model p = 0.002). The full 24-hour behavioral profile for each treatment is shown in Figure 1, and the day-to-night shift in grazing is illustrated in Figures 2 and 3.

Drinking Behavior and Water Intake
Counting every animal-day (including 13 animal-days without drinking), ad libitum animals (W+) drank 1.8× as often as restricted animals (3.14 vs 1.75 events/animal/day; rate ratio = 1.8; p < 0.001). The Poisson model was underdispersed (dispersion ratio = 0.427); the generalized Poisson GLMM gave the same conclusion (rate ratio = 1.81; p < 0.001; dispersion φ = 0.39). Daily water intake per animal was 22.6 L in W+ and 19.1 L in W− (difference = 3.5 L; p = 0.173), a difference that was not significant with group × period as the experimental unit. Within bouts, W− animals took more sips per event (18.8 vs 15.5; negative binomial (glmmTMB, nbinom2), Poisson dispersion ratio = 3.6; p = 0.047), and their bouts were not significantly longer (geometric mean 21.1 s vs 17.8 s; ratio = 1.18; p = 0.141), at the same sip rate (W+: 0.832 sips/s; W−: 0.82 sips/s; p = 0.811).

Shade Area Use
Among S+ animals, those with restricted water (S+W−) spent a significantly greater proportion of daytime scans in shade compared with ad libitum animals (59.6% vs 54.7%; p < 0.001), despite having access to the same silvopastoral area (Figure 7). The difference came mainly from the morning: between 07:00–11:00h, S+W− animals were in shade 10.5 percentage points more often than S+W+ on average, whereas between 13:00–18:00h the two treatments differed by only -0.6 points on average. Shade use peaked at 15:00h. The 12:00h and 17:00h scan blocks were excluded for both treatments because S+W− animals were in the trough corridor (recorded as sun) during watering. This shows a trade-off: water restriction made animals leave shaded areas during hot hours.

Sensitivity to the Experimental Unit
Reducing each outcome to its 16 group × period means and analysing them as a Latin square (6 error df) gave the same conclusion at the 0.05 level for 51 of 55 tests (Table 47a). The 4 that differed were shade for daytime other (LS p = 0.030; mixed model p = 0.052), water for water intake (LS p = 0.047; mixed model p = 0.175), water for sips per event (LS p = 0.304; mixed model p = 0.045) and shade × water for sip rate (LS p = 0.076; mixed model p = 0.035) (Table 47b). The group:period variance was ≈ 0 in the mixed models for daytime other, nighttime grazing, drinking events / day and water intake; for these outcomes the Latin-square test on group × period means is the more conservative reference.
